units.la: STUDIOSIS P. P. & L. L. Salvere, ac benè rem gerere Academicè.
units.tr: To the students P. P. and L. L., greetings, and may you carry on your affairs in the manner of the Academy.

units.la: Laßicum dictum est, & classicè etiam verum: Ubi definit Philosophus Practicus, ibi incipit Jurisconsultus. Hæc prima, hæc secunda, hæc tertia causa, cur vestro ordini hunc sermonem sacrum esse jubeam, secutus exemplum Demosthenis palliati, & Catonis togati, quorum ille rogatus, quid in dicendo foret primum, quid secundum, quid tertium? Pronunciationi sive actioni primas, huic secundas, huic tertias dedit: Hic verò interpellatus, quem in primis, quem in secundis, quem in tertiis amaret? Fratri Cœpioni primitias sui amoris, eidem secundinas, eidem tertianas detulit: Neque aliâ mente nos fraternis studiis, Studio, inquam, Philosophiæ Practicæ & Jurisprudentiæ, easdem, quæ sicut in œconomiâ domesticâ studiorum combinata immane quantum prosunt, ita malè luxata immane quantum obsunt. Quemadmodum enim geminæ stellæ Castoris & Pollucis salutares, prosperiquè cursus prænunciæ putantur, solitariæ verò minaces, & malæ scævæ: Item gemella hæc studia, prout congeminant, aut non congeminant Ledæi hi fratres, ovo prognati eodem. Valete Musarum & Gratiarum corcula.
units.tr: It is a laconic saying, and also true in the classical sense: where the practical philosopher ends, there the jurist begins. This is the first, this the second, and this the third reason why I order this sacred discourse to be dedicated to your order, following the example of Demosthenes the cloaked and Cato the togaed, of whom the former, when asked what was first in speaking, what second, and what third? He gave first place to delivery or action, second to this, third to that. The latter, when questioned whom he loved first, second, and third, gave the first-fruits of his love to his brother Cepio, the second share to the same man, and the third to the same man. In the same spirit we bring these fraternal studies, I mean the study of Practical Philosophy and of Jurisprudence, which, when combined in the household economy of learning, help immensely, and when badly dislocated, harm immensely. For just as the twin stars of Castor and Pollux are thought to be saving and to foretell a prosperous course, while the solitary ones are threatening and bad omens, so these twin studies, as the sons of Leda, born of one egg, either join together or fail to join. Farewell, little hearts of the Muses and the Graces.
