units.tr: Daniel Berckringer's Encomium of the Truly Architectonic Study of Politics

units.la: AEquè fortean gravem & grandem vobis committere videbor [?]olœcismum Politicum, AUDITORES, quòd ego, homo Philosophus, qui usquè in umbrâ, nunquam in luce atque oculis Reipublicæ vixi, nullamquè ejus partem domi militiævè attigi, de Majestate Studii Politici hinc ad vos verbigerari præsumam, æquè, inquam, gravem & grandem solœcismum Politicum, atque olim, illud humanæ sapientiæ terrestre oraculum Socrates, solœcismum Oeconomicum, qui, cùm vix quinque minarum rem in patrimonio haberet, Critolaum nihilominùs artem opulescendi docuit, faciem tenùs insipienter, verà interim re sapientissimè, ut non immeritò de triumvirali collegio sapientum, Sophocles sapiens, Euripides sapientior, Socrates verò sapientissimus, domi audierit inter suos: Phormio hinc Peripateticus solœcismum Ethico-Polemicum, quem, cùm apud Hannibalem, exulantem exilium in Asiâ, aliquot horas de officio imperatorio, dequè deque omni re castrensi, superciliosissime diseruisset, isque forte rogatus esset, quid de ipso sentiret, fertur hoc scommatio immo commate extemporali excepisse, multos quidem se vidisse deliros senes, sed qui magis quam Phormio deliraret, vidisse neminem, credo, quod de re militari, docte ille quidem, verum alieno tempore & loco, verba caederet, ipse militiae experimentalis indoctissimus, ut qui ne pictam quidem unquam in pariete imaginem aciei oculis usurpasset suis, tacite huic insinuans illud Pyrrhi Epirotae: Ne mihi de militia judicium sibi sumat, cujus aures armorum strepitus, tubarumque clangor, non circumstrepuit circumsonuitque. Cujus moniti reverentia victus Machiavellus, jussus a Magno Duce Hetruriae, qui tum forte delectum militum habebat, exercere cohortem levis armaturae armis, suae sibi inmilitiae conscius, eam provinciam detrectavit, togato consilio in re sagata usus, licet Marte scripto nemini cederet, neipsi quidem Marti.
units.tr: Perhaps I shall seem to you, Listeners, to commit a political solecism just as grave and great, in that I, a philosopher who have always lived in the shade and never in the light and gaze of the commonwealth, who have touched no part of its affairs at home or in war, presume to speak to you here about the majesty of the political study. I say it is just as grave and great a political solecism as once Socrates, that earthly oracle of human wisdom, committed as an economic solecism. Though he had hardly five minae of property, he nonetheless taught Critolaus the art of growing rich. He appeared foolish on the surface, yet in reality was most wise, so that, not undeservedly, among the triumvirate of wise men (Sophocles the wise, Euripides the wiser, Socrates the wisest), he was heard at home among his own people. Hence Phormio the Peripatetic committed an ethico-polemical solecism. When he had spent some hours, while Hannibal was in exile in Asia, lecturing most haughtily to Hannibal about the duties of a commander and about every military matter, and was happened to be asked what he thought of himself, he is said to have answered with an impromptu jibe or quip: he had seen many deranged old men, but had never seen anyone more deranged than Phormio. He was learned, I grant, but he chattered about the art of war at the wrong time and place, while being himself most unskilled in practical warfare, one who had never once set eyes on even a painted picture of a battle line on a wall. He was tacitly hinting at that saying of Pyrrhus of Epirus: let no one claim a judgement about war for himself whose ears the clash of arms and the blare of trumpets have never rung around and resounded about. Warned by this reverence, Machiavelli was ordered by the Grand Duke of Tuscany, who then happened to be raising a levy of soldiers, to drill a company of light infantry in arms. Conscious of his own inexperience in the field, he declined that charge, relying on civilian counsel in a military matter. Yet by his written work on war he yielded to no one, not even to Mars himself.

units.la: Verum enimvero, Auditores, quid vetat, quo minus in hoc orationis nostrae proscenio, facto Socratico comparemus dictum Isocraticum, dicam, an Iso-Socraticum, magni illius Isocratis, patris eloquentiae, cujus domus, quasi publicus ludus oratorius, patuit cunctae Graeciae. Quid ergo ille? Ille vero cuidam sapientulo curiosius percontanti, qui fieret, ut, cum ipse ad dicendum minus minusque foret aptus, alios tamen ad dicendi studium redderet aptissimos? In arena reposuit, eo se id facere modo, quo cotes, quae, cum ipsae sint exortes secandi, ferrum tamen acutum reddant. Næ acute acutius acutissimè! Quod verbum, sui purgandi ergò, loco proteli, tantus vir, cujus una oratio viginti talentis olim veniit, curiositati rogantis oppo-suit, idem nos ejus exemplo opponamus sanè adver-sariorum cavillationibus, & posthabitis eorum famili-aribus cavillis, almam Politicen nostram, quà Epito-micam, quæ nudis partim præceptis partim exemplis absolvitur, accommodam tyronum tyrocinio, quà A-podicticam, complectentem & τὸ ὅτι sive suppositum, & τὸ διότι sive propositum, neque vera tantùm confir-mantem, sed etiam falsa infirmantem, accommodam veteranorum studiis, quà Paraeneticam, adhibentem argumenta, non solùm Logica, quibus fidem astruat rebus dubiis, sed etiam Ethica & Pathetica, quibus in audientium animos se Sirenum more illatebret, hosquè ad officii functiones quasi accensâ face inflammet, ac-commodam utrorumque doctis desideriis, quà Empi-ricam, experimenta horum omnium in Reipublicæ gubernatione capessentem, accommodam virorum lumbis & lateribus, omnes digné condignis mactemus laudibus, ita tamen, ut nec Empiricæ Politicæ affinga-mus alienas, nec Dogmaticæ detrahamus suas, quæ communior, copiosior, cognitu facilior, securior, in comparationis libripendio. Communior est Dogma-tica seu Doctrinalis Politica Empirica seu Experimen-tali, vel eo nomine, quòd melioribus mollioribusque litteris, & per naturam, & per fortunam, operam na-vare
units.tr: But truly, Listeners, what forbids us, on the stage of this oration, to set beside the Socratic deed the saying of Isocrates (or should I say Iso-Socrates?), that great man, father of eloquence, whose house, like a public school of oratory, lay open to all Greece? What did he do? When a certain rather inquisitive little sage asked him how it was that, though he himself was less and less fit for speaking, he nonetheless made others most fit for the study of speaking, he replied in the arena that he did it in the way whetstones do. Though they cannot cut themselves, they make iron sharp. Sharp, sharper, sharpest! This word, put forward in his own defence, that so great a man, whose single speech once sold for twenty talents, set against the curiosity of his questioner. So let us, following his example, set against the cavils of our adversaries, and, scorning their familiar jibes, duly praise all of our kindly Politics: the Epitomic, which is completed partly by bare precepts and partly by examples, suited to the apprenticeship of beginners; the Apodeictic, which embraces both the "that" [τὸ ὅτι], the supposition, and the "why" [τὸ διότι], the proposition, confirming not only true things but also refuting false ones, suited to the studies of veterans; the Paraenetic, which employs not only logical arguments by which it establishes belief in doubtful matters, but also ethical and emotional ones, by which it creeps into the minds of hearers in the manner of the Sirens and kindles them to the performance of their duties as with a torch set alight, suited to the learned desires of both; and the Empiric, which takes up the experiments of all these in the government of the commonwealth, suited to the loins and sides of men. Let us praise all of them worthily, yet in such a way that we neither attach foreign features to Empiric Politics nor strip Dogmatic Politics of its own. The Dogmatic or Doctrinal Politics is more common, more copious, easier to know, and safer when weighed in the balance of comparison. It is more common than the Empiric or Experiential, for this reason above all: that the opportunity to devote one's labour to the finer and gentler letters, both by nature and by fortune, is open to as many as possible, whereas public offices belong to a few persons.

units.la: * libri vare liceat quàm plurimis, publicæ contrà functiones sint pauculorum capitum : Copiosior quoque est illa hâc, eò quòd in Politicorum tabulis &membranis oceanus quidam consiliorum atque eventuum se nobis offerat, cùm è converso infra numerum', saltem intra numerum, sint, quæ in brevissimo, & angustis admodum limitibus circumsepto, vitæ humanæ curriculo, ex usu quis haurire potest: Sed & cognitu facilior eadem, quoniam minoris multò dividiæ & laboris, domi per ocium Musis suis operari, quàm in Republicâ Danaidum, quod ajunt, pertusum dolium aquâ implere semper, Ixionis cruciarii rotâ circumagi semper, Sysyphiq; fatale saxum volvere semper: Securior deniq; est, quia candidati hujus studii, absque periculo, immò metu periculi, politicis incubrationibus intendunt, procul à Jove, ideoqué & à fulmine, cùm contrà illi, qui rei dant nomen publicæ, ferè lupum auribus, ursum naribus teneant, ut quibus cum bestiâ illâ multorum capitum res sit, quæ ut venter aures non habet, etiam tum, cùm habet. Sit sanè hoc quasi propylæum & vestibulum præsentis orationis meæ, Auditores. Agite, componite jamnunc togam, atque ipsam Regiam Reginæ Politices bonis mecum avibus ingredimini. Ecce autem mox à limine, immò in limine, obtutui nostro se offert conclave instructum non unum, Conclave, quod vocant, Antiquitatis, Conclave Necessitatis, Conclave Dignitatis, Conclave Utilitatis, Conclave Voluptatis, Conclave Difficultatis. Perambulabimus, nisi grave est, aut percurrecurremus potius singula raptim. Neque enim in omnibus æqualiter dabitur sistere gradum, ne mole & majestate visendorum absorbeantur visentes. Atque adeò, Antiquitatem hujus Studii quod concernit, næ illud Codro & Titanibus antiquius, ut quod eosdem cum societate humanâ habeat natales, quâ cûm bonâ fide, & pueravit, & adolevit, & consenuit, facto gradatim à conjugio ad familias, à familiis ad collegia, à collegiis ad corpora, à corporibus ad universitates, ab universitatibus ad Respublicas, à Rebuspublicis ad totum genus humanum, uti progressu, ita regressu, eâ ferè ratione, quâ fluvios se in mare, & hoc in fluvios, exonerare videmus κυκλογενέσει quâdam. Sed quia non est reperire, qui primam hanc & ultimam veritatem Politicam vocet in dubium, ideò à Nativitate hujus Studii rectâ me viâ confero ad huic proximam Necessitatem, quæ ex priori prædicato, tanquam ex fonte, quasi per derivationem condescendit. Quòd si enim alma vitæ societas, ejusque alumna communicatio, est necessaria, ut est, ejus quoque societatis & communicationis mutuæ cognitio, necessaria utique fuerit ex hoc capite, adeoque si Politia de necessitate, etiam Politica. Cùm enim Politia vertatur in imperantium & parentium ordine, quomodo quæsò rectè imperabitur & parebitur, si imperandi & parendi prudentiâ, inde destituantur principes, hinc cives? Destituuntur autem absque Politicâ. Inde principes. Ut enim agrum & vineam non nisi perito cultori permittimus, nemo se nauclero credit, dit, ignaro maris & fluctuum, ne imperitum quidem tibicinem conviviis adhibemus, & grandem illam Reipublicæ navem, tot animas vehentem, imperantis peritiâ periclitari patiemur? Sed ne corpus quidem credimus, nisi Medico experto, qui illud, ex tam variis membris, tam contrariis organis, venis, arteriis, visceribus, musculis, humoribus, spiritibus compaginatum, arte sua curet, omnesque ejus partes ad analogiam harmoniam & symmetriam reducat, & corpus civitatis, quod tanto sublimius, quàm corpus humanum, quanto dignius, consulere omnibus, quàm singulis, imperantis supinitate periclitari patiemur? Hinc deinde autem cives, qui si parendi prudentiâ destituantur, dictumfactum turbatur Respublica, mercatura in fraudes & impostu-ras definit, naviculatoria in piraticam, agricultura in prædatoriam abit, bellum in latrocinia, judicia in rapinas, artes liberales in heroicam desidiam, religio in superstitionem, sacra in ceremonias degenerant, quod ubi fit, lucernam mero meridie cum Diogene accendas licet, & Rempublicam quæras in Republicâ, sicut ille olim homines hâc accensâ inter homines. Ac quoniam artes & disciplinæ ex objecto subjecto & fine, uti amant loqui Scholæ, æstimari solent, ubi de earum dignitate & præstantiâ anquiritur, pauca mihi etjam super hoc argumento, in nostro hoc argumento, commentanda sunt, verùm pauca scilicet, eò quòd de dignitate nunquam satis disseras pro dignitate. Ecquænam ergò illa, circa quæ augustum hoc studium, tantanquam circa centrum suum, vertitur, annon, si objectum personale spectes, homo, animal nobilissimum, cæteris animantibus antecellens, consideratus non in ordine ad se, sed in ordine ad civitatem, in uno tertio, immò primo, nempè cum perpetuâ relatione ad τὸ ἀρχεὶν καὶ ἀρχεσθαι, quibus duobus vinculis uterque mundus, quasi pugno manus, continetur, & ὁ μακρόκοσμος sive major, & ὁ μικρόκοσμος, sive minor, epitome majoris? Annon, objectum hinc reale si respicias, (philosophum hic magis ago, quàm Oratorem,) Rerumpublicarum constitutio, constitutarum administratio, administratarum conservatio? Magistratuum, legum, juris, domi forisque descriptio? Armorum hinc, fœderum, pœnarum, præmiorum, onerum & subsidiorum publicorum, succedanea ut condispositio ita condispensatio? At qui bonum, quò communius, hoc utique clarius & præclarius, ut quod ambitu suo utrumque bonum, & particulare, & singulare, includat: Quòd si bonum, quò communius, hoc præclarius, etjam studium, quod, quo universalius, hoc regalius ex hoc fundamento. Ecquinam præterea, qui studium hoc, velut proprium & peculiare, in possessione suâ habuerunt, annon Principes Viri, inter Hebræos, Moses, David, Daniel, Nehemias, πολιτικώτατοι? Inter Græcos, Nestor, Ulysses, Archytas, Pythagoras, Timæus Locrus, Lysis Tarentinus, Clisthenes, Pericles, Demosthenes, Socrates, Plato, qui duplicem Rempublicam descripsit, unam exemplarem, in libris de Republicâ, publicâ, alteram ad exemplum, in libris de legibus, imitatione fortan Phidiæ, qui in Jovis & Minervæ statuis ideam perfectæ pulchritudinis effinxit, imitatione Zeuxis, qui Helenam pictunus muliebris formæ præstantiam è quinque puellis, imitatione Ciceronis, qui perfectum oratorem è turbâ oratorum, imitatione Xenophontis & Virgilii, qui perfectum item principem, alter in Cyro, alter in Æneâ, graphicè delineaverunt: A Platone hinc Aristoteles, quem autor est Laërtius, præter duos libros de Republicâ Platonis, & tres de legibus, alios de Republicâ legibus urbibus regno, conscribillâsse: Ab utroque porrò Xenocrates, Theophraftus, Xenophon, Æschines, Heraclides Ponticus, Demetrius Phalereus, Isocrates, & universè, tam Academici, quàm Peripatetici, qui ob eximiam rerum magnarum scientiam κατ' ἐξοχὴν Politici sunt nominati, Stoicis & Epicuræis ut excipiendis ita exceptis, quorum alteri attigerunt & ipsi quidem hanc Philosophiæ partem, sed multa attulerunt absurda, atque à communi vitâ abhorrentia, nonnunquam etiam flagitiosa fœcennina & turpia, alteri verò ne attigerunt quidem hunc locum: Inter Romanos porrò Decemviri, Fabii, Catones, Scipiones, Lælii, nominatim par ingenium Imperio Romano Cicero, & mox Seneca, plus aliquid semper dicens, quàm dicit, Christianè, si legas ut Paganum, Paganicè, si legas ut Christianum, Plutarchusque, thesaurus ille eruditionis, cujus unius operibus universalem jacturam cæterorum scriptorum rum, si Codicem Dei & Justiniani excipias, resarciri posse autumat nonnemo: Et ponè præallegatos autores alii de Politicorum tribu & censu, numero ac nomine infiniti, ad doctum hoc nostrum usque ævum, in quo vitam & spiritum ducimus, quorum scripta Politica si in unum volumen quis affectatâ diligentiâ redigere vellet, næillud portentosæ molis corpus foret, inquè id ritè quadraret vetus & verum, verum & vetus verbum, μέγα βιβλίον μέγα κακόν, magnus liber magnum malum. Ecquis denique iterum iterumquè laudati, sed nunquam satis laudandi studii finis, (de fine externo loquor, non interno,) annon publica salus, quâ unâ omnes omnium & singulorum salutes continentur? Unde non leve iterum momentum ac pondus accedit huic studio, quoniam præstantissimi finis cognitio ad præstantissimam pertinet facultatem, qualis citra controversiam nostra hæc, etiam hoc nomine, quæ ideò augusto honoris titulo Platoni Ἐπιταχτικὴ Aristoteli verò Ἀρχιτεκτονικὴ audit, princeps & domina quòd sit reliquarum facultatum atque scientiarum, quibus leges dat, & jura dictat, quasvè adeò architectonicè disponit, aliis imperans, aliarum causâ imperans, alteris ad exemplum patrisfamiliâs, ad exemplum servi atriensi alteris, eâdem operâ pro imperio præcipiens, & quas in civitate disciplinas doceri conveniat, & quas quemque discere, & quatenus has discere, & cui bono? Quas in civitate disciplinas doceri conveniat? Neque enim patitur Politica, ut domi foveantur antur artes, aut inutiles, ne cives illis occupati ab utilibus studiis avocentur, aut perniciosæ, quæ vergant ad corruptionem, vel animi, vel corporis, vel fortunarum, ceu sunt, Sophistica, Declamatoria, Versificatoria, Critica nugatoria, Empirica, Rabularia, Quodlibetaria, Mimi, Pantomimi, Archimimi, Cybeitistæ, Petauristæ, Petaminarii, Funambulones, Neurospastæ, & qui dicuntur Agyrtæ Græcis, Latinis Ærusicatores seu Æsculatores, universéque totum genus τῶν θαυματοποιῶν: Magia hinc, Necromantia, Astrologia Judiciaria, Physiomantia, Chiromantia, Pythonica Hariolorum, Disciplina Auguralis, Nundinatoria, Fœneratoria, Lenonia, Tabernaria, Unguentaria, Dulciaria, & si quæ sunt mali hujus commatis plures. Hujus augusti Imperii Politici vi domi usus Lycurgus, omnes quondam supervacaneas artes è Republicâ Spartanâ uno impetu exterminavit, Minos è Cretensi Rhetorculos, Plato è suâ Poëtastros, Romani Medicastros philosophastros Musicastros, Ludiones item & Chaldæos, Saul Magos, Lacedæmonii coquos Unguentarios, & Fœneratores, nunc Lombardos, omnes, quasi strumam & pestem Reipublicæ præsentissimam. Quas item disciplinas quemque discere conveniat? Cùm enim non ex quolibet ligno fiat Mercurius, nec omnes æquè sint idonei ad quamlibet facultatem, sed alius ad hanc, alius ad aliam, magis natus vel factus, rectè næ bis rectè facit Politica, quòd studiis diis civium suorum consulit, habitâque ratione ingeniorum, ortus, status, quemque id studii sectari jubet, quò ipsum vocat & invitat, sua vel natura, vel conditio. Neque enim, qui animo sunt ad militiam & arma compositο, ad scholas & fabricas relegandi, neque item, qui litteris habent accommodata ingenia, ad castra vel rastra amandandi. Ex hoc fundamento, Romanis quondam moribus, civi, jure quem vocant optimo maximo, sutoriâ & sartoriâ interdictum, nostris quin etiam moribus hodieque nobili mercaturam exercere, aut coenacula riam facere, jus non est. Neque verò artes solùm praefinire Politica, sed & loca ac spacia, instrumentaque harum, in quibus & ex quibus illæ doceri discique debeant. Olim certè Jus Civile Romanum non licuit profiteri publicè, nisi tribus locis orbis Romani, Romæ videlicet, quæ de Constitutione Justiniani Imperatoris habuit Professores Jurisprudentiæ quaternos, Byzantii item & Berythi, quarum urbium singulæ binos. Sed & reliquas artes non temerè alibi profiteri licuit, ludosque earum aperire, quàm in utraque Romà Athenis Alexandriæ & Tharsi. Quod dixi de locis, idem tenuit & in libris, de ejusdem Justiniani constitutione, quâ de nullos per Imperium tractare alios Juris libros licebat Provincialibus, nisi qui ab ipso conscripti, aut saltem jussu ipsius conscripti forent. Justinianum imitatus alter Justinianus Lotharius, jura Romana, post quingentorum ferè annorum exilium, in scholas & forum postliminiò reduxit, legesque Romanas, cum blattis & tineis bellum gerentes, in lucem protraxit, constituto Bononiæ Juris professore Irnerio, quem exceperunt Azo & Bulgarus, magna in familia Jurisprudentum nomina. Quatenus hinc eadem disciplinas discere conveniat? Ut cùm præcipit Politica, ne studiosa pubes multò maximam ætatis partem in Grammatici aut Rhetoris ludo, philosophivé gymnasio ducat, verùm maturo & benè cocto consilio se conferat ad Facultates, atque inde porrò ad Ecclesiam, vel Rempublicam, cui privato parentum, & publico patriæ voto, est votita: Dum item v. g. Imperatoriæ, quæ manus Reipublicæ, imperat, quò ducere exercitum, quomodo eum regere, quando manus conserere, quo pacto victoriâ uti debeat: Oratoriæ, quæ lingua Reipublicæ, quid, quatenus, quomodo, quo loco & tempore, sit dicendum, ut ad clepsydram dicat Orator, ne affectus moveat, ne concionem cogat, ne turbas vocis fulmine concitet, id quod legibus cautum olim erat Athenis contra τὺς σοφιστὰς: Oeconomicæ, quæ pes Reipublicæ, quis modus esse debeat in possessione agrorum, famulorum, in permutando, vendendo, emendo &c. Quo fine denique eas discere conveniat? Nempè egregii publici causâ, cujus promovendi ergò, in arce Reipublicæ, quasi in speculâ, sedens heroina nostra, inde ex alto despicit & prospicit, ne vel artes depravatæ doceantur, vel artes bonæ depraventur,
units.tr: ...to be permitted to as many as possible, whereas the public functions belong to only a few. The former is also more abundant than the latter, because in the tables and parchments of the political writers a kind of ocean of counsels and outcomes presents itself to us, whereas conversely the things that one can draw from the very brief course of human life, hemmed in by very narrow limits, are fewer than that number or at least within it. Moreover, the same study is easier to know, since it requires far less trouble and labour to work at one's Muses at home in leisure than in the Republic, where, as they say, one must always fill the Danaids' leaky jar with water, always turn the wheel of Ixion's torment, and always roll Sisyphus's fated stone. Finally, it is safer, because the candidates of this study devote themselves to political meditations without danger, or rather without fear of danger, far from Jove and therefore from the thunderbolt; whereas those who give their name to public affairs must hold the wolf by the ears and the bear by the nostrils, since they have to do with that many-headed beast which, like the belly, has no ears, even when it has them. Let this, learned hearers, be as it were the propylaeum and vestibule of my present oration. Come, put on your togas, and enter with me, under good omens, into the very royal hall of the Queen of Politics. But see, straight from the threshold, or rather on the threshold, there presents itself to our view a chamber furnished not with one but with several: the chamber, as they call it, of Antiquity, the chamber of Necessity, the chamber of Dignity, the chamber of Utility, the chamber of Pleasure, the chamber of Difficulty. We shall walk through them, unless it is troublesome, or rather we shall run through the individual rooms in haste. For we shall not be allowed to halt equally in all of them, lest those who view them be swallowed up by the bulk and majesty of the things to be viewed. And so, as far as the antiquity of this study is concerned, it is older indeed than Codrus and the Titans, since it has the same birth as human society, with which in good faith it has been a child, has grown up, and has grown old; having progressed gradually from marriage to families, from families to colleges, from colleges to bodies, from bodies to universities, from universities to commonwealths, from commonwealths to the whole human race, and in returning again, in much the same way as we see rivers discharge themselves into the sea and the sea into rivers, by a certain cyclogenesis [κυκλογενέσει]. But since no one can be found who would call this first and last political truth into doubt, I therefore hasten by a straight path from the birth of this study to its neighbour, Necessity, which descends from the former predicate as from a fountain, as it were by derivation. For if the nourishing society of life, and the communication that nourishes it, is necessary, as it is, then the knowledge of this society and of mutual communication must necessarily also be necessary on this head, and so, if politics is of necessity, so is political science. For since a commonwealth turns on the order of those who command and those who obey, how, I ask, will one rightly command and rightly obey, if rulers are deprived of the prudence of commanding, and citizens of the prudence of obeying? But they are deprived of it without political science. The rulers first. For just as we do not entrust a field or a vineyard except to a skilled cultivator, and no one trusts himself to a sailor ignorant of the sea and its waves, nor do we admit an unskilled flute-player to our banquets, shall we allow that great ship of the commonwealth, carrying so many souls, to be endangered by the skill of a ruler? Nor do we trust even the body except to an experienced physician, who by his art cures it, compounded as it is of so many varied limbs and such contrary organs, veins, arteries, viscera, muscles, humours and spirits, and who reduces all its parts to analogy, harmony and symmetry; and shall we allow the body of the state, which is as much more sublime than the human body as it is more worthy to consult all rather than each, to be endangered by the sloth of a ruler? Then in turn the citizens, who, if they are deprived of the prudence of obeying, then as soon as it is said, the commonwealth is thrown into confusion: commerce degenerates into frauds and impostures, seafaring into piracy, agriculture passes into plunder, war into brigandage, the courts into robbery, the liberal arts into heroic idleness, religion into superstition, and sacred things into ceremonies. When this happens, one may light a lamp at high noon with Diogenes and seek a commonwealth in the commonwealth, just as he once sought men among men with his lamp lit. And since the arts and disciplines are usually estimated, as the schools love to say, from their object, subject and end, when inquiry is made into their dignity and excellence, a few things must also be commented upon on this argument in our present argument, but only a few, because one never speaks sufficiently of dignity in proportion to its dignity. What then are those things around which this august study revolves, as around its own centre? Is it not, if you look at the personal object, man, the most noble animal, surpassing the other living creatures, considered not in relation to himself but in relation to the state, in the one third, or rather first, namely in perpetual relation to to rule and to be ruled [τὸ ἀρχεὶν καὶ ἀρχεσθαι], by which two bonds each world, as a fist is held by a hand, is contained, both the greater world [ὁ μακρόκοσμος], or macrocosm, and the lesser world [ὁ μικρόκοσμος], or microcosm, an epitome of the greater? Is it not, if you look at the real object from here (here I am acting more as a philosopher than as an orator), the constitution of commonwealths, the administration of those constituted, the conservation of those administered? The description of magistrates, laws and rights at home and abroad? Hence the arrangement, and the disbursement, of arms, treaties, penalties, rewards, burdens and public subsidies, as their substitutes? But the good, the more common it is, the clearer and more excellent it is, since it includes within its compass both the particular good and the singular good. And if the good, the more common it is, the more excellent, then also the study which, the more universal it is, the more regal it is from this foundation. Moreover, who else has held this study as their own and peculiar possession? Were they not princely men, among the Hebrews, Moses, David, Daniel, Nehemiah, most political [πολιτικώτατοι]? Among the Greeks, Nestor, Ulysses, Archytas, Pythagoras, Timaeus of Locri, Lysis of Tarentum, Clisthenes, Pericles, Demosthenes, Socrates, and Plato, who described a double commonwealth, one exemplary, in the books on the Republic, and the other modelled on it, in the books on the Laws, perhaps in imitation of Phidias, who in the statues of Jove and Minerva expressed the idea of perfect beauty; in imitation of Zeuxis, who painted Helen's surpassing feminine beauty from five girls; in imitation of Cicero, who fashioned the perfect orator from a crowd of orators; in imitation of Xenophon and Virgil, who likewise sketched the perfect prince, the one in Cyrus, the other in Aeneas. From Plato, Aristotle, as Laertius is the authority, besides the two books of Plato's Republic and the three on the Laws, wrote others on the Republic, on laws, on cities, on kingdoms. From both of these in turn Xenocrates, Theophrastus, Xenophon, Aeschines, Heraclides Ponticus, Demetrius of Phalerum, Isocrates, and in general both the Academics and the Peripatetics, who on account of their outstanding knowledge of great affairs were named politicians par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]; the Stoics and the Epicureans being both received and excluded in the same way, of whom the former indeed touched upon this part of philosophy, but brought forward many absurd things, far removed from common life, sometimes even shameful, obscene and base; and the latter did not even touch upon this topic. Among the Romans, moreover, the Decemvirs, the Fabii, the Catos, the Scipios, the Laelii; and by name Cicero, who was an equal genius to the Roman Empire, and afterwards Seneca, who always says something more than he says, speaking like a Christian if you read him as a pagan, and like a pagan if you read him as a Christian; and Plutarch, that treasury of learning, by whose works alone someone maintains that the universal loss of other writers can be made good, if you except the Code of God and of Justinian. And after the writers cited above, others concerning the rank and assessment, the number and name, of political writers, infinite in number, down to this learned age of ours, in which we draw life and breath, whose political writings, if anyone with affected diligence wished to reduce into a single volume, that would be a body of monstrous bulk; and that old and true saying fits it aptly: a great book is a great evil [μέγα βιβλίον μέγα κακόν]. Finally, who is not aware of the end of this study, again and again praised but never praised enough (I speak of the external end, not the internal), namely public welfare, in which alone the welfare of all and of each is contained? From this a further and no slight weight and importance accrues to this study, since knowledge of the most excellent end belongs to the most excellent faculty; and such is beyond controversy our faculty, also on this account, which for that reason bears the august title of honour: for Plato it is called Epitactic [Ἐπιταχτικὴ], but for Aristotle Architectonic [Ἀρχιτεκτονικὴ], being the prince and mistress of the other faculties and sciences, to which it gives laws and dictates rights, and which it arranges architectonically, commanding others, and commanding for the sake of others; ordering some by the pattern of the father of a household, others by the pattern of the steward of a servant; at the same time, by its command, prescribing both which disciplines it is fitting to teach in the state, and which each person should learn, and how far he should learn them, and to what good end. Which disciplines is it fitting to teach in the state? For politics does not allow the arts to be fostered at home which are either useless, lest citizens occupied with them be diverted from useful studies, or pernicious, which tend to the corruption of mind, body or fortunes; such as sophistry, declamation, versifying, trifling criticism, empiricism, wrangling, quodlibetical disputation, mimes, pantomimes, archimimes, cybisistae, rope-dancers, acrobats, petaminarii, tightrope walkers, puppeteers, and those called agyrtae by the Greeks and aerusicatores or aesculatores by the Latins, and in general the whole kind of the wonder-workers. Then magic, necromancy, judicial astrology, physiognomy, chiromancy, the Pythonic prophecy of soothsayers, the discipline of augury, the trade of the market-place, usury, pimping, the tavern trade, the perfumers' and the confectioners' arts, and whatever other ills of this sort are numerous. By the force of this august political empire, Lycurgus once used it at home, and with one stroke drove out all superfluous arts from the Spartan commonwealth; Minos drove the little rhetoricians from Crete, Plato drove the petty poets from his own state; the Romans drove out the quacks, the petty philosophers and the petty musicians, likewise the jugglers and the Chaldeans; Saul drove out the magicians; the Lacedaemonians drove out the cooks, the perfumers and the moneylenders, and now the Lombards, all of them, as the most pressing scrofula and pestilence of the commonwealth. Which disciplines, again, is it fitting for each person to learn? For since Mercury is not made from every kind of wood, and not all are equally suited to every faculty, but one is born or made more fit for this and another for that, politics rightly, yes, rightly so, takes care of the studies of its citizens, and, having regard to their talents, their origin and their station, bids each one pursue that study to which his nature or condition calls and invites him. For neither should those who are by disposition inclined to military service and arms be relegated to the schools and workshops, nor likewise should those whose talents are suited to letters be sent away to the camp or the plough. On this foundation, under Roman customs, it was once forbidden to a citizen of the best and greatest right, as they call it, to practise cobbling and tailoring, and even by our own customs today it is not lawful for a nobleman to exercise commerce or to keep a shop. Nor does politics only prescribe the arts, but also the places and spaces, and the instruments of these, in which and from which they ought to be taught and learned. Formerly, certainly, Roman civil law could not be publicly professed except in three places of the Roman world: at Rome, namely, which under the Constitution of the emperor Justinian had four professors of jurisprudence; likewise at Byzantium and at Berytus, two in each of these cities. And the other arts too could not be professed elsewhere, or their schools opened, except in the two Romes, Athens, Alexandria and Tarsus. What I have said of places holds also for books, under the same constitution of Justinian, by which it was permitted to no provincials throughout the empire to handle any other books of law except those written by himself, or at least written by his command. Imitating Justinian, another Justinian, Lothair, after an exile of nearly five hundred years, led the Roman laws back again into the schools and the forum, as if restored by the right of return, and brought the Roman laws to light, waging war with the cockroaches and the moths, a professor of law, Irnerius, having been established at Bologna, whom Azo and Bulgarus succeeded, great names in the great family of jurists. To what extent it is therefore fitting to learn these disciplines? As when politics prescribes that studious youth should not spend the greater part of its age in the school of the grammarian or the rhetorician, or in the philosophers' gymnasium, but should, with mature and well-digested counsel, betake itself to the faculties, and from there further to the Church or the commonwealth, to which it has been vowed by the private wish of its parents and the public wish of its country. Meanwhile, for example, the military art, which is the hand of the commonwealth, commands: whither to lead an army, how to govern it, when to join hands, in what manner it ought to use victory. The art of oratory, which is the tongue of the commonwealth: what, how far, how, in what place and at what time, one ought to speak, so that the orator speaks as long as the water-clock allows, does not stir the passions, does not gather a crowd, does not excite the tumult of the voice like a thunderbolt; which the laws of Athens once took care to forbid against the sophists. The economic art, which is the foot of the commonwealth: what measure ought to be observed in the possession of fields and servants, in exchanging, selling, buying, and so on. Finally, for what end it is fitting to learn them? Namely, for the sake of the outstanding public good, the promotion of which our heroine, sitting in the citadel of the commonwealth as on a watchtower, looks down and looks out from on high, lest either depraved arts be taught, or good arts be corrupted.

units.la: [Marginal notes at left edge are cut off and only partly legible; not transcribed.] ventur, neu quo casu Litterator in Litterionem, Orator in vitilitigatorem & clamosum Stentora, Historicus in Fabulatorem, Dialecticus in Sophistam, Physicus in Magum, Medicus in Paracelsistam, Jurisconsultus in Rabulam, Theologus in Hæreticum vel Schismaticum, transfabeat. Interest interest siquidem Reipublicæ, ne artes serię utiles & bonæ, in vana inutilia impia desinant, sive liberales illæ sint, sive illiberales, necessariæ tamen, aut, si desinant, nova incude diffigantur. Quorsum modico ante laudatus Lycurgus, cùm Rempublicam legibus formaret, opificia non ejecit, sed modum his adhibuit, putà, ut fabri lignarii, lectulos, sellas, & id genus alia, conficerent illi quidem, verùm sine supervacuis ornamentis. Quod ipsum, & in poculis, & in calceis, & in vestibus, observitari voluit. Neque enim ferundæ illæ maleferiatorum opificum ineptiæ, qui cervos ligneos, currentes muscas, reptantes serpentes fabrefaciunt, & talibus nugis Rempublicam replent, quod de Callicrate & Mermecyde, Æropo item Macedone Ælianus, horum omne studium in conficiendis quadrigulis muscariis eburneolis, operis longè subtilissimi, lucernulisquè ac mensulis effabricandis, occupatum fuisse. Minùs quin etiam ferundi, qui cùm Aristomacho Solensi maximo conatu maximas nugas agunt, quo de Albertus Magnus, quòd in muscarum naturâ rimandâ, pulicumquè saltibus dimetiendis, (Auditum admissi risum teneatis amici!) totos sexaginta annos consumserit, dignus, meo judicio, qui cùm suis muscis & pulicibus sexagies de ponte dejiciatur. Sed & Athenienses, Lycurgi exemplo, non exturbârunt luxurientes Poëtas, verùm licentiam tantùm conviciandi novo legum obice represserunt, ut Reipublicæ suæ consulerent. Næ laudabili temperamento Politico! Tantum de dignitate. Jam utilitas hujus studii tanta est, ut si mihi forent centum linguæ, oraquécentum, ferrea vox, non tamen dicendo illa exæquari posse videatur. Præterquam enim, quòd hæc disciplina præscribat imperantibus virtutes imperatrices, parentibus obtemperatrices, utrisque moderatrices, quarum felici conjugio nihil Reipublicæ salutarius, uti vel Scipionis exemplo militari docemur, qui cuidam sciscitanti, quâ re fretus classem in Africam trajicere pararet, huic exerto digito ostendisse perhibetur trecentos viros armatos, se præluforiè exercentes ad proelium, eâdemquè Pharon, sive turrim excelsam mari imminentem, addidisseque, nullum horum esse, qui non conscensâ turri illâ se præcipitem in mare sit daturus, siquidem id jussisset, Quodquè omnes vitæ humanæ & Reipublicæ partes constituat curet salvet, adeò ut, absque câ sit, tota hominum universitas nihil futura sit aliud, quàm merus Cyclopismus, magnum, inquam, latrocinium, & rabies plusquam ferina, in quâ nec religio, nec Dei cultus, nec fides, nec aræ & foci, nec existimatio cujusquam aut fama, sed nec necessaria vitæ subsidia & præsidia, nec denique corpora & vita, tutum hospitium unquam inveniant: Etiam aliis disciplinis præclara comra commoda larga manu sumministrat. Theologo enim conducit ad Politiæ Mosaicæ intelligentiam, ordinis ecclesiastici descriptionem, officiorum sacrorum & civilium distinctionem, utquế sciat Theologiæ sacratum caput, quid juris competat, quid incompetat, imperanti in Civitate Dei, ne vel in excessu, vel in defectu, offendat, tribuendo ei plus minusvé, quàm scientiæ & conscientiæ forum permittit. Jurisconsulto eadem suggerit communia principia juris ac legum. Neque enim negari potest, saltem non debet, Ethicam & Politicam esse illos fonticulos, de quibus Jurisprudentiæ rivuli manant. Etenim cùm leges Reipublicæ sint attemperandæ, sive novas condere, sive mutare veteres, sive jam usu receptas interpretari gestias, potenè est id fieri sine cognitione Politicæ, quæ parens ac domina legum, quarum Jurisperitus est interpres, ut qui respondeat de jure secundum leges. Atque hæc hæc videtur esse causa non postrema, quare hæc duo sororia studia mutuas sibi invicem tradant operas, asperrimeque à se invicem possint divelli, nec multò magis quis esse (præfiscinè dixerim,) perfectus Jurisconsultus sine Politicâ, quàm Politicus sine Jurisprudentia. Cùm enim pro tribus Reipublicæ partibus in tres adæquatè partes tributur Politica laxè sumta, quarum una propriè attinet ad magistratum, diciturque Νομοθετικὴ Legislatoria, altera ad Consilia, diciturque Βουλευτικὴ Consiliaria sive Senatoria, tertia ad Judicia, diciturque Δικαστικὴ Judiciaria, Jurisprudentia, quam Jurisconsulti profitentur, tentur, quà Confulti Juris, ut sic Politicæ pars est, cùm eodem habitu legislator legem sanciat, & Jurisconsultus interpretetur, qui si omnes tres partes conjungat, ut sæpè usuvenit, quin Politici hic talis nomen sibi arrogare possit non arroganter, dubium non est, dum Politicam presse, atque in rigore, quod ajunt, sumtam, à Jurisprudentiâ bonâ fide distinguat modò, quæ Politica disciplina ut distincta ita distinguenda à Iurisprudentiâ, fide rationum, quas laudat Montecatinus Ferrariensis in suâ ad Aristotelis Πολιτικὰ præfatione. Contraham in compendium, auro saltem aurichalco contrà non cara verba autoris, idquè compendii causâ.
units.tr: [Marginal notes at left edge are cut off and only partly legible; not transcribed.] venture, or in some case a grammarian turns into a mere wordsmith, an orator into a wrangler and a noisy Stentor, a historian into a fabulist, a dialectician into a sophist, a natural philosopher into a magician, a physician into a Paracelsian, a jurist into a pettifogger, and a theologian into a heretic or schismatic. For it is indeed of concern to the commonwealth that the useful and good arts should not degenerate into vain, useless and impious trifles, whether they are liberal or illiberal, yet necessary; or, if they do so degenerate, that they be pinned down and reforged on a new anvil. This is why Lycurgus, praised a little earlier, when he shaped the commonwealth by his laws, did not banish the crafts but set a limit to them: for example, that carpenters should make bedsteads, chairs and that kind of thing, but without superfluous ornament. He wanted this same restraint observed in cups, shoes and clothing. Nor should we tolerate the absurd products of those wretched craftsmen who make wooden stags, running flies and crawling serpents, and fill the commonwealth with such trifles. Ælian reports this of Callicrates and Mermecydes, and likewise of Aeropus the Macedonian, whose whole effort was spent on making little four-horse chariots of flies, a work of the most delicate skill, and tiny lamps and tables. Less tolerable still are those who, with the greatest effort, accomplish the greatest trifles, like Aristomachus of Soli. Of him Albertus Magnus is reported to have spent a full sixty years investigating the nature of flies and measuring the leaps of fleas (you may hold back your laughter, friends, at what I hear!). In my judgement he deserves to be thrown off a bridge sixty times along with his flies and fleas. But the Athenians too, following Lycurgus' example, did not drive out the wanton poets; they only restrained their licence to heap abuse by a new barrier of laws, in order to look after the good of their commonwealth. Oh, what a praiseworthy political moderation! So much for its dignity. Now the usefulness of this study is so great that, even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths and a voice of iron, I would still seem unable to express it in words. For, apart from the fact that this discipline prescribes to rulers the virtues that command, to parents those that obey, and to both those that moderate, and nothing is more beneficial to the commonwealth than their happy union, as we are taught even by the example of Scipio in military matters. When someone asked him on what he relied when he was preparing to ferry a fleet to Africa, he is said to have pointed with an outstretched finger to three hundred armed men exercising themselves for battle in the practice field, and to have added the Pharos, the high tower overlooking the sea, saying that none of these men would fail to climb that tower and throw himself headlong into the sea, if he ordered it. And this discipline arranges, takes care of and preserves all the parts of human life and of the commonwealth, so that without it the whole human race would become nothing but pure Cyclopism, a great robbery, and a rabies more than beastly, in which neither religion, nor the worship of God, nor faith, nor altars and hearths, nor the reputation or good name of anyone, nor even the necessary supports and safeguards of life, nor finally bodies and life itself, would ever find a safe refuge. It also supplies other disciplines with splendid advantages in abundance. For it is useful to the theologian for understanding the Mosaic polity, for describing the ecclesiastical order, and for distinguishing sacred from civil offices, so that he may know what right belongs to the sacred head of theology and what does not, and may not offend the ruler in the City of God, either by excess or by deficiency, in assigning to him more or less than the forum of knowledge and conscience allows. To the jurist it suggests the common principles of law and of statutes. For it cannot be denied, or at least it ought not to be, that Ethics and Politics are those little springs from which the streams of jurisprudence flow. Indeed, since the laws of the commonwealth must be tempered to it, whether one wishes to enact new ones, to change old ones, or to interpret those already received by custom, can this be done without knowledge of Politics, which is the parent and mistress of the laws, whose interpreter the jurist is, as one who answers about right according to the laws? And this seems to be no small reason why these two sister studies lend each other mutual help, and can scarcely be separated from one another, nor is anyone (may I speak without ill omen) a perfect jurist without Politics, any more than a politician without jurisprudence. For since Politics, taken broadly, is divided into three parts corresponding to the three parts of the commonwealth, of which one belongs properly to the magistrate and is called Legislative (νομοθετική), another to counsels and is called Deliberative (βουλευτική), that is, consultative or senatorial, and the third to judgments and is called Judicial (δικαστική), and since jurisprudence, which the jurists profess, is, in so far as the jurist, as the expert in law, is part of Politics, when the same person enacts the law as legislator and interprets it as jurist, it is no doubt that, if someone joins all three parts together, as often happens, he may not arrogantly claim for himself the name of a politician, provided that he keeps Politics, taken strictly and in its exact sense, as it is said, distinct in good faith from jurisprudence. This political discipline, as it is distinct, so must it be distinguished from jurisprudence, on the grounds of the reasons which Montecatini of Ferrara praises in his preface to the Politics of Aristotle. I shall condense this into a summary, taking the author's words, gold if not brass, and not dear words in the opposite sense, and I do so for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Philosophiæ, inquit, proprium est, omnium rerum causas primas investigare: Hoc facit Politica, edisserens omnium rerum, quæ ab ipsâ considerantur, causas primas, non item Iurisprudentia, quæ non scrutatur primas causas eorum, quæ tractat, verùm leges tantùm, quæ observandæ sunt, docet, causâ non adhibitâ, aut adhibitâ quidem, ast non primâ, tum paucarum legum, non omnium, præterquè hinc consilium institutumquè: Ergò! Et mox: Si Politica, inquit, pertinet ad Iurisprudentiam, vel intelligetur Prudentia Iuris Romani, vel Prudentia Iuris cujusvis: Si illa, tunc omnes regiones & gentes, quæ Romano jure non utuntur, (sunt verò iste multò plures, quàm quæ utuntur, atque inter eas nonnullæ artibus moribus legibus politissimæ,) omnes, quæ impostærum non utentur, omnes, quæ hactenus non sunt usæ, omnes, quæ antè hoc jus conditum eo caruerunt, carent carebunt caituræ sunt omni Politicâ, quare nec civiles societates ullas, quæsine Politicâ, sive civicivili ratione, esse nequeunt, habent habuerunt habebunt: Sin hæc, quoniam civitates convenit teneri legibus, næ illi, qui af-severant, non differre Politicen à Iurisprudentiâ, innumeras Politicas cudunt, cùm una tantùm sola simpliciter esse debeat, quanquam multæ interim dentur formæ Rerumpublicarum, quemadmodum una tantùm sola & simpliciter est Medicina, licet multæ sint medendi rationes, variatæ locis, variatæ temporibus, variatæ ætatibus, variatæ temperamentis. Adhuc: Si, inquit, probatas Respublicas, & celebres legumlatores, qui has constituerunt, memoriâ repetas, non Iurisperitos illos, sed Philosophos fuisse invenies, Mercurium Trismegistum, Rhadamantum, Androdamantem, Epimenidem, Onomacritum, Philolaum, Zaleucum, Charondam, Lycurgum, Draconem, Pittacum, Solonem, cuius potissimum leges Romani pro suis descripserunt. Hactenus ille, non magis à nobis sine sacrilegio hoc loco tacendus, quàm nunquam satis loquendus Tacitus, arte hoc agens, quod non agit, & non agens, quod agit, communis ille Apollo Politicorum, quem penè turpiter præterieram in Syllabo Politicorum, cuius ipse est α & ω. Sed & prænominata disciplina Politica non parum bonæ utilitatis affert, & Oratori, & Poëtæ, quibus argumentum, illi perorandi, ut qui in iisdem commilitet rebus, in quibus Politicus, huic poëtandi, suppeditat, quoniam Comœdiæ poëtarum, fictè quidem, at non vanè, sunt speculum vitæ domesticæ, Tragœdiæ verò publicæ, at Politica utriusq;, quæ Politica porrò & Historica tradunt sibi invicem quasi per manus lampada eruditionis. Etenim historia promit exempla singula, quorum regulas & canones generales exhibet Politica, quæ inde Regularis Historiæ nomen accepit, sicut Historia nomen Exemplaris Politicæ, Historiâ persequente facta, Politicâ verò jus factorum. His tantis tamquè enormibus compendiis Studii Politici, quo reliqua omnia studia sibi demeruit, moti Stoici, meo judicio, non inconcinnè, nec inappositè, cùm Philosophiæ trium partium, Logicam sepimento, Physicam arboribus conferrent, fructibus Ethicam & Politicam similes finxerunt, comparatâ horto universâ Philosophiâ: Alii, domestico hoc eorum exemplo, testæ seu pùtamini Logicam, albumini Physicam, vitello Ethicam & Politicam assimilare, ipsi ovo iterum comparatâ Philosophiâ: Alii denique, animali collatâ Philosophiâ, ossibus quidem ac nervis Logicam, carni & sanguini Physicam, animo verò Ethicam, cum sororio Politicæ studio, comparare. Quid multis? Non quidem, quò minùs febre laboremus, nec quò minùs faciamus naufragium, sed nec quò minùs vastemur terræmotibus, & affligamur fulminibus, hoc præstat Politica, at facit alia pensiora. Et quoniam omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci, merito præter utilitatem eximiam hujus studii, ejusdem quoque suavitatem de meliori commendamus, hoc magis, quia alibi nescio quomodo cum floribus leguntur spinæ, hic verò absque spinis flores, hoc est, veræ & germanæ voluptates, non umbratiles, inaniquè quâdam speciè coloratæ.
units.tr: It is proper to philosophy, he says, to investigate the first causes of all things. Politics does this, setting out the first causes of all the things it considers. Jurisprudence does not, since it does not examine the first causes of the things it treats, but only teaches the laws that are to be observed, with no cause given, or with a cause that is not first. Moreover, it teaches only some laws, not all. Therefore... And soon after: If politics belongs to jurisprudence, it must be understood either as the prudence of Roman law or as the prudence of any law whatever. If the former, then all regions and peoples that do not use Roman law (and there are far more of these than of those that use it, and among them some very refined in arts, morals and laws) are, and will be, and have been, and always will be, without any politics, all those who will not use it, all who have not used it until now, all who lacked it before this law was made. Hence they have no civil societies, which cannot exist without politics, or civil reason. But if the latter, since states ought to be bound by laws, then those who maintain that politics does not differ from jurisprudence coin countless politics, whereas there ought to be only one, simply, although there are many forms of commonwealths, just as there is only one medicine, simply, although there are many methods of healing, varied by places, times, ages and temperaments. Again: If you call to mind the approved commonwealths and the famous lawgivers who established them, you will find that they were not jurists but philosophers: Mercury Trismegistus, Rhadamanthus, Androdamas, Epimenides, Onomacritus, Philolaus, Zaleucus, Charondas, Lycurgus, Draco, Pittacus, and Solon, whose laws the Romans chiefly copied for their own. So far he; a passage not to be passed over here without sacrilege, any more than Tacitus, that common Apollo of the politicians, can ever be spoken of enough. He acts in this matter by art, doing what he does not do, and not doing what he does; I had almost shamefully passed him by in my Syllabus of politicians, of which he is the alpha and omega. The aforesaid political discipline also brings no small benefit to the orator and the poet. For the orator it supplies arguments for his speeches, since he deals with the same matters as the politician; for the poet it supplies subject matter for poetry. Comedies of the poets, feigned yet not idly, are a mirror of domestic life, and tragedies of public life, but politics belongs to both. Politics and history in turn hand on to each other, as it were from hand to hand, the torch of learning. For history offers single examples, whose rules and general canons politics sets forth, and politics thus took the name of the regulative history, just as history took the name of the example of politics: history pursues deeds, politics the law of deeds. Moved by these great and immense advantages of political study, by which it has earned the service of all the other studies, the Stoics, in my judgment not inappropriately or unsuitably, when they compared philosophy in its three parts to a garden, likened logic to the hedge, physics to the trees, and ethics and politics to the fruits. Others, using this domestic example of theirs, compared philosophy to an egg: logic to the shell or membrane, physics to the white, ethics and politics to the yolk. Others finally compared philosophy to an animal: logic to bones and sinews, physics to flesh and blood, ethics to the soul, together with politics as its sister study. What more is there to say? Politics does not prevent us from suffering fever, nor from being shipwrecked, but nor does it prevent us from being laid waste by earthquakes and struck by lightning; this it does not provide, but it does other, weightier things. And since he who mixes the useful with the pleasant has carried every vote, we rightly commend this study for its pleasantness as well as its outstanding usefulness, all the more because elsewhere, somehow, thorns are read along with flowers, whereas here there are flowers without thorns, that is, true and genuine pleasures, not shadowy ones, nor coloured by some empty appearance.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim Suave mari magno, turbantibus æquora ventis, E terrâ magnum alterius spectare laborem, Non quia vexari quemquam sit jucunda voluptas, Sed quibus ipse malis careas, quia cernere suave est:
units.tr: For just as it is pleasant, when the winds stir up the sea, to watch from land another's great struggle: not because anyone's distress is a delight, but because it is sweet to see from what evils one oneself is free.

units.la: Ita suave, immo nectare & ambrosiâ suavius, in portu politices videre vada, æstuaria, syrtes, scopulos ex scopulis, absque scopulo privatæ offensionis tamen. Quid enim quæsò aptius ad delectationem lectoris, quàm rerum varietates, fortunæque vicissitudines intelligere, quæ etsi optabiles aliis in experiundo non sunt, in legendo tamen nobis sunt jucundæ. Habet habet quippè alieni doloris secura recordatio oblectionem apud eos, qui nullâ perfuncti propriâ molestiâ casus aliorum sine ungue in ulcere intuentur. Atque adeò, quid suavius, quàm totius orbis terrarum leges & Respublicas animo percurrere, earumque conversiones cum veris causis cognoscere, inque speculâ politicâ quasi in coràm veterem spectare fabulam, quæ in omnibus totius orbis terrarum partibus, nonnisi mutatis personis, agitur? Quid deinde autem acceptius, quàm bene rem gerere bono publico, & cùm omne genus humanum, tùm patriam, suâ sapientiâ domi contra cives, foris contra hostes, tueri? Quid denique gratius, quàm unum præ cæteris sapere in civitate, quasique oraculum aliquod consuli, locoque numinis in civitate haberi inter concives, coli, observari, omnibusque elogiorum titulis quasi floribus conspersi. conspergi? Et quem non suaviter delectet Cyrus Major, lectus à pueris collusoribus comicus rex, itemque augustulus ille Augustinus, dum illum videt officia civilia, hunc ecclesiastica, inter turbam ludentem ludibundum dividere? Quem non mystica illa arbor Nabuchodonosoris, quae ad coelum usque vertice suo pertingebat, totumque orbem terrarum obumbrabat, cujus folia fuerunt longe pulcherrima, fructus multo uberrimi, quibus desaginabatur & suppinguescebat, quicquid fuit usquam animalium, cujus in frondibus atque ramis omne genus volucrum certatim nidificabat, sub quorum ramorum umbraculis otiose quietem, & captabat, & capiebat, rex animantium homo, in utram vis aurem dormiens, oculumque conquinisccns utrumque, quae arbor imago fuit florentis imperii, non in alio fundo nata, quam Politico. Sed scilicet, quemadmodum lana quosdam colores semel & simul ducit, quosdam vero, nisi saepius macerata & recocta non perbibit: Gemino modo Politica, multa egens maceratione, & concoctione multa, ob sui difficultatem, quam tamen facile obscurant atque obruunt, à nobis laudatae, iterumque laudandae, antiquitas, necessitas, dignitas, utilitas, jucunditas hujus professionis & studii, sed maxime omnium interim dignitas & praestantia, eo quod veteri proverbio, aut veriverbio potius, δύσκολα καὶ καλά, difficilia, quae pulchra. Unde vero illa difficultas, unde? Illa vero protuberat ex duplici fonte, altero praeceptoceptorum, inprimis specialium, (nam generalia obvia sunt, aperta sunt, plana sunt,) idque ob mare circumstantiarum, quae circumstantiae omne hic ferunt punctum, & utramque, quod ajunt, faciunt paginam, altero vero usus, qui operosissimus, ita ut vix humerosus Atlas, & lacertosus Hercules, huic oneri sint ferundo, quod immane quantum aggravant, ratione subjecti, mores ipsorummet, tam imperantium, quam parentium, ratione vero objecti seu strati, res illis domi foris{que} subjectae. Ecquales enim ii, qui sedent ad puppim Reipublicae, annon, licet Deorum nomen & numen ferant inter homines, aspectu muneris, quod vicario titulo gerunt in terris, tales non οὐσίαι, sed ἐξουσίαι, annon vasa fragilia, testacea, lutea? Annon saepius, quasi torrente aliquo abripiuntur, vel caecitate mentis, vel vi perturbationum, vel violentia & vehementia vitiorum,
units.tr: Thus it is sweet, indeed sweeter than nectar and ambrosia, to watch from the harbour of politics the shallows, estuaries, quicksands, and rocks beyond rocks, without the rock of a private injury. For what is more apt, I ask you, for the reader's delight than to understand the variety of affairs and the vicissitudes of fortune? Though these are not things one would wish to undergo oneself, we find them pleasant to read about. For the safe recollection of another's pain brings enjoyment to those who have suffered no personal hardship and look upon the misfortunes of others without having a finger in the sore. And what is sweeter than to run through in the mind the laws and commonwealths of the whole world, to learn their changes and their true causes, and to watch from the vantage of politics, as if from a box, the old play which, with only the actors changed, is performed in every part of the world? What is more pleasing, next, than to manage affairs well for the public good, and to protect the whole human race and, above all, one's country by one's wisdom, at home against citizens and abroad against enemies? What is finally more gratifying than to be the one man above the rest in a state who is consulted like some oracle, who is held in the place of a divinity among his fellow citizens, is worshipped and observed, and is strewn, as with flowers, with every title of praise? And who would not be delighted to see Cyrus the Elder, who was chosen as king by his playmates in a game of boys, and that little Augustus, the boy Augustine, dividing between the two of them, while one plays the civil and the other the ecclesiastical role, among a crowd of playing children? Who would not be delighted by that mystical tree of Nebuchadnezzar, which reached with its top to heaven and overshadowed the whole world, whose leaves were most beautiful and whose fruit very abundant, by which every animal there was fed and fattened, in whose foliage and branches every kind of bird nested in rivalry, and under whose shady boughs man, king of the animals, sought and found quiet rest, sleeping on whichever ear he pleased and closing both eyes? That tree was an image of a flourishing empire, which grows in no other soil than that of politics. But surely, just as wool takes up some colours at once and all together, while others it will not absorb unless it has been often soaked and boiled again, so politics, which needs much soaking and much boiling because of its difficulty, is in a twofold way praised by us, and must be praised again: its antiquity, necessity, dignity, usefulness, and pleasantness, but above all its dignity and excellence, because of the old proverb, or rather true saying, [δύσκολα καὶ καλά] difficult things are beautiful. But whence comes that difficulty, whence? It springs from a double source: one is the precepts, especially the particular ones (for the general ones are obvious, open, and plain), and this because of the sea of circumstances, which circumstances carry every point here and make up both sides of the page, as they say; the other is practice, which is most laborious, so that scarcely broad-shouldered Atlas or brawny Hercules would be equal to bearing this burden, which they weigh down immensely: by reason of the subject, that is, the morals of the rulers themselves as well as of parents, and by reason of the object or material, the affairs placed under them at home and abroad. For what sort of men are those who sit at the stern of the commonwealth? Are they not, although among men they bear the name and majesty of gods, in view of the office they hold on earth by vicarious title, not substances [οὐσίαι] but authorities [ἐξουσίαι]? Are they not fragile vessels, of earthenware and clay? Are they not most often swept away, as if by some torrent, either by blindness of mind, or by the force of passions, or by the violence and vehemence of vices,

units.la: Non aliter, quam qui adverso vix flumine lembum Remigiis subigit, si brachia forte remisit,
units.tr: Just as a man who, rowing a small boat against a strong current, has happened to slacken his arms,

units.la: Atque illum in praeceps prono rapit alveus amne; sive ipsis deliberandum sit de futuris, sive judicandum de praeteritis & praesentibus, dum praeferunt interdum scorias auro, cortices medullae ligni? Ecquales deinde autem ii, qui sedent ad proram Reipublicae, quique remos agunt, per foros cursitant, sententiam exhauriunt, annon homines; omnium animalium animal maximè intractabile, quo nullum morosius, nullum majori arte tractandum, ut quod neque servitutem neque liberbertatem ferre possit, sub leni imperio lasciviens, sub aspero fatiscens, sub utroque contra imperantem insurgens, siqué conatus ejus metu superioris potentiæ compescatur, querelis se ulciscens, adeò, ut omnibus animalibus facilius sit imperare, quàm homini, citiusque inveniatur vir fortis, qui hostem superet, quàm qui civem, annon ita? Ecquales hinc porrò res utrisque substratæ, annon singulares, ideoque infinitæ, saltem indefinitæ, variisque circumstantiis quasi fasciis involutæ, atque ita quidem involutæ, ut humanis consiliis sæpenumerò explicari nequeant, nisi Deus Ἀντὶ μηχανῆς, cujus auspicis auxilium implorandum, ut olim rustici invocârunt numen Cereris, antequam terræ mandarent semina, nisi, inquam, Deus nobis præsentem opem ferat, suâque scientia nostram insciitiam, potentiâ impotentiam sarciat, atquè non raró res sint sic satis expeditæ, nec deest etiam magistratui animus expediendi, sed nec subditis adsit animus impediendi, tamen eventus earum multoties reguntur occultis causis, ita ut optimè consulta pessimè cadant, præclarissimique conatus in spongiam incumbant, atque in nervum erumpant vel tandem, Jovis interim taxillis semper cadentibus benè in hâc vitæ humanæ Tragico-Comœdiâ, & Comico-Tragœdiâ. Cæterùm, quæ tumultuariè consignavi de difficultate hujus studii, ea non in sinistram accipi velim partem, Auditores, quasi animo absterrendi hæc ziza-nia seram, verùm in dexteram, ut ipsa difficultas stimulum multum addat confligentibus cum his asperitatum salebris, hoc majorem, quò illa minor, quàm Philosophiæ Speculativæ, quæ spinetis & senticetis est refertissima, subtilitates ex subtilitatibus, non parturiens tantùm, sed pariens, quo nomine vapulant apud cascos maleferiati satores & seminatores earum, Protagoras, Nausiphanes, Parmenides, Zeno, Pyrrho, & Heraclitus, ὁ σκοτεινὸς, ad cujus scripta intelligenda Delio natatore, qui in summa aquâ natare erat doctus, opus esse ducebat Socrates, ne quis illis legendis præfocaretur, omnes, quòd noctem seu tenebras ex composito inducerent rebus, nimiamque nescio quo gargarismo, affectarent subtilitatem, & vel non præferrent facem suis auditoribus, lucernâ sub modio positâ, vel animi oculos his effoderent. Quòd si quæ reliquiæ difficultatum præter expectationem superant in animo discentis Politicè, quæ nebulam immò nubem videantur offundere oculis ejus, tum sanè, meo judicio, proximum fuerit, ut quemadmodum Themistocles Nisiphilum, Pericles Anaxagoram, Dio Platonem, Philippus Macedo, & Epaminondas Græcus, Lysin Tarentinum, Alexander Magnus Aristotelem, Scipio Polybium & Panætium, Cicero Nigidium, Phocio Chabriam, Aristides Clisthenem, Ptolemæus Philadelphus Demetrium Phalereum, alii alios, à docto suo latere habuerunt, ita & ipse in suo comitatu habeat aliquem horum sacrorum ducem, qui ipsum Mercurialiter manuducat ad metam civilis institutionis. Atque huc huc etiam potenter conferent modernis moribus Lectiones Publicæ, & Collegia Privata, quæ hac occasione quasi prætereundo commendo, eò quòd plus valeat viva vox, quàm muta lectio, meliusquè & fidelius hærent, quæ auditione, quàm quæ lectione, accipimus. Certè rarissimi omni seculo fuerunt αὐτοδίδακτοι, homines privatim docti, qui aliquod eruditionis singularis nomen meruerint, adeoquè vix tot numero ex omni numero, quot sunt Thebarum portæ, & divitis ostia Nili. Atque ita, (quæ res benè vobis, benè verò mihi vortat,) quasi aliud agens, vos compendiò deduxi per Augustam Regiam Almæ Reginæ Politicæ, Auditores. Quòd si avetis scire, quem me feram, quemquè locum in augustà familià ejus teneam? Respondebo desideraturientibus, Politicus sum, & Disciplinam Politicam publicà autoritate è cathedrà hic doceo, ut sacris Politicis à benè multo tempore initiatus, ita alios in dies initians, verùm Theoreticè, non Practicè, uti in vestibuloque hujus sermonis multà cum ingenuitate sum professus, ut qui de duobus cruribus Politices altero tantùm gaudeam, nempè Arte, non item alteo, nempe Usu. Felices verò, iterum iterumquè felices in Reipublicæ administratione, quibus utrumque crus habere datum, quales Civilistæ & Statistæ, qui Praxin Politicam cum Theoriâ Politicâ, Politicam, inquam, Experimentalem cum Doctrinali sociant, cum præsentissimo Reipublicæ compendio atq; interesse: Eccur? Quia enim fortiores causæ fortiorem edunt dunt effectum, funiculusque duplex non ita facile rumpitur ac simplex, & vero etiam praestat duabus ancoris niti, quàm unâ, plurisque adeò est Doctor Utriusque Juris, quàm Unius, & Baro, & Comes, quàm aut Baro, aut Comes, similiterque Politicus, & Academicus, & Epidemicus, in argumento praesenti, quâm aut Academicus, aut Epidemicus. Infelices contrà, iterumque iterumque infelices, in ejusdem rei tractatione publicae, qui, vel Theoriam tantùm Politicam percallent, ut Homines Umbratici, domi oculati, foris caeci, vel praxin tantùm Politicam, ut Homines Curiales, quales olim Athenis, Miltiades, Cimon, Conon, quorum Schola fuit Curia & Forum, unde Demades orator rogatus, quem in prudentiâ civili acquirendâ magistrum habuisset, reposuit, quòd tribunal Atheniensium, nostris moribus Pragmatici, quos sic vocant in circulis, vel neutram, persuade, nec Theoriam Politicam, nec Praxin Politicam, uti Sophistae olim, & Oratores Logodaedali, qui schemata solùm, & larvas rerum, neglectis corporibus, exuviasque pro carne, reduvias pro unguibus, obtruserunt, illi imperitis & incautis adolescentibus in scholis, hi rudi plebeculae in foro, nunc verò Aulici & Seculares, omnium qui sunt horarum homines, & Politi potiùs, (complementeurs,) quàm Politici, quorum Politicam quondam Graeci populariter meretricem, à demerendis hominum animis & studiis, hodiè Itali Graecissantes Cortisana vocant. Et certè, ut vasa colligam, si dicendum siet, quod res est, malim sanè sane inter famosas Thaidas castam Susannam aut Penelopen habere, quàm huius commatis Politicum, interquè Alcibiadem solito civiliorem, & Dionem solito inciviliorem, Cleomenem aliquem moribus civilem, gerentem se πολιτικῶς, Ciceronis verbo, hoc est, ut ego interpretor, nec Gnathonicè, nec Thrasonicè, verùm Thrasybulicè, jungendo exemplo Thrasybuli τῷ θεάσεα τὴν βουλὴν, ut absque adulationis fuco, sive Gnathonismo, ita absque jactantiæ vento, sive Thrasonismo.
units.tr: and the channel swiftly carries him headlong down the stream, whether they must deliberate about the future, or judge the past and present, while they sometimes prefer dross to gold and bark to the pith of wood? What sort, then, are those who sit at the prow of the commonwealth, who ply the oars, run about the forums, and drain opinion? Are they not men, the most intractable of all animals, than which none is more capricious and none needs to be handled with greater skill, since it can bear neither servitude nor liberty, grows frisky under gentle rule, faints under harsh rule, and under either rises against the ruler; and if its attempts are checked by fear of a higher power, it takes revenge with complaints. So it is easier to rule all other animals than man, and a brave man who conquers an enemy is found more quickly than one who conquers a fellow citizen. Is that not so? What sort, further, are the matters laid under both: are they not singular, and therefore infinite, or at least indefinite, and wrapped up with various circumstances as with bandages, and wrapped so tightly that they often cannot be unfolded by human counsels, unless God, the god from the machine [Ἀντὶ μηχανῆς], whose auspices must be implored, as of old the farmers invoked the power of Ceres before entrusting seed to the earth? Unless, I say, God brings present help to us, and by his knowledge makes up for our ignorance and by his power for our impotence? And though often affairs are thus sufficiently prepared, and the magistrate does not lack the will to carry them through, nor do the subjects lack the will to obstruct them, yet their outcomes are often governed by hidden causes, so that the best-considered measures fall out worst, and the most distinguished efforts collapse into a sponge and burst at last into a sinew, while meanwhile the dice of Jupiter always fall well in this tragicomedy and comitragedy of human life. But what I have jotted down in a disorderly way about the difficulty of this study, I would not have you, listeners, take in a bad sense, as if I were sowing these tares to frighten you off; rather take it in a good sense, so that the difficulty itself adds a strong spur to those who struggle with these rough places of difficulty, all the more because it is smaller than that of speculative philosophy, which is most crowded with thickets and brambles, producing subtleties out of subtleties, not merely bearing them but begetting them. For this reason Protagoras, Nausiphanes, Parmenides, Zeno, Pyrrho, and Heraclitus the obscure [ὁ σκοτεινὸς] are thrashed by the cunning, ill-trained sowers and planters of them; and to understand their writings, Socrates thought one needed a Delian swimmer, one trained to swim in deep water, lest anyone be drowned in reading them. All of them, because they deliberately brought darkness upon things and affected I know not what excessive subtlety with some kind of gargling, either did not hold up a torch before their hearers, putting the lamp under the bushel, or gouged out the eyes of their minds. But if any remnants of difficulty beyond expectation remain in the mind of the student of politics, seeming to pour a mist, indeed a cloud, over his eyes, then in my judgement it would be best for him to do as Themistocles had Nisiphilus, Pericles Anaxagoras, Dion Plato, Philip of Macedon and Epaminondas the Greek had Lysis of Tarentum, Alexander the Great had Aristotle, Scipio had Polybius and Panaetius, Cicero had Nigidius, Phocion had Chabrias, Aristides had Clisthenes, and Ptolemy Philadelphus had Demetrius of Phalerum; each had others at his side as a learned companion, and so too he should have in his company one of these sacred guides, who leads him by the hand, Mercury-like, to the goal of civil training. To this end public lectures and private colleges, as they are conducted in modern manners, will also contribute powerfully, which I commend here in passing on this occasion, because the living voice is worth more than silent reading, and what we receive by hearing sticks better and more faithfully than what we receive by reading. Certainly the self-taught, men learned in private who have earned some singular name for learning, have been very rare in every age, scarcely as many in number as the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the rich Nile. And so, (may this turn out well for you, and well for me,) as if doing something else, I have briefly led you, listeners, through the august palace of the nourishing Queen Politics. But if you wish to know what kind of man I am, and what place I hold in her august household? I answer those who long to know: I am a politician, and I teach the discipline of politics publicly from this chair, having been initiated into the political rites for a good long time and so initiating others day by day; but theoretically, not practically, as I frankly professed at the threshold of this discourse, since I enjoy only one of the two legs of politics, namely the art, and not the other, namely the practice. Happy indeed, again and again happy in the administration of the commonwealth, are those to whom it has been granted to have both legs, such as the civil lawyers and statesmen, who join political practice to political theory, experimental politics, I mean, to doctrinal, with the most immediate benefit and interest of the commonwealth. Why? Because stronger causes produce a stronger effect, a double rope does not break as easily as a single one, and indeed it is better to rest on two anchors than on one; thus one is more a Doctor of Both Laws than a Doctor of one law, and more a baron and count together than either a baron or a count; and similarly, in the present subject, a politician who is at once academic and a man of the world is more than either an academic or a man of the world alone. Unhappy, on the other hand, and again and again unhappy in the handling of this same public matter, are those who either know political theory only, like men of the shadows, sharp-eyed at home and blind abroad, or know political practice only, like men of the court, such as once at Athens Miltiades, Cimon, and Conon, whose school was the senate-house and the forum. Hence when Demades the orator was asked whom he had as a teacher in acquiring civil prudence, he replied that it was the tribunal of the Athenians. Or, to be persuaded of the other alternative, that neither theory nor practice is known, like the sophists of old and the logodaedalus orators, our pragmatists, as they are called in the circles today, who put forward only the shapes and masks of things, neglecting the bodies, offering cast-off skins for flesh and hangnails for nails; the former to inexperienced and unwary youths in the schools, the latter to the crude common folk in the forum. But now there are courtiers and worldlings, men of all hours, and polite men (complimenters) rather than politicians, whose politics the Greeks once popularly called a harlot, from its winning over men's minds and pursuits; today the Italians, who ape the Greeks, call it a courtesan. And indeed, to wrap things up, if it must be said as it is, I would far rather have a chaste Susanna or Penelope among the notorious Thaïses than a politician of this kind; and rather than a man who is more civil than usual like Alcibiades, or more uncivil than usual like Dion, I would have some Cleomenes, civil in manners, conducting himself politikōs, in Cicero's word, that is, as I interpret it, neither Gnathonically nor Thrasonically, but Thrasybulically, adding the example of Thrasybulus, who saw the council [τῷ θεάσεα τὴν βουλὴν]; so that, free of the paint of flattery, or Gnathonism, so also free of the wind of boasting, or Thrasonism.

units.la: sane inter famosas Thaidas castam Susannam aut Penelopen habere, quàm hujus commatis Politicum, interquè Alcibiadem solito civiliorem, & Dionem solito inciviliorem, Cleomenem aliquem moribus civilem, gerentem se πολιτικῶς, Ciceronis verbo, hoc est, ut ego interpretor, nec Gnathonicè, nec Thrasonicè, verùm Thrasybulicè, jungendo exemplo Thrasybuli τῷ θεάσει τὴν βουλὴν, ut absque adulationis fuco, sive Gnathonismo, ita absque jactantiæ vento, sive Thrasonismo.
units.tr: Surely it is easier to find a chaste Susanna or Penelope among the notorious Thaides than a politician of this kind. Alcibiades was more civil than usual, Dion more uncivil than usual, and there was some Cleomenes, civil in manners, who conducted himself politically [πολιτικῶς], to use Cicero's word. That is, as I interpret it, he acted neither in the manner of Gnatho nor of Thraso, but in the manner of Thrasybulus, joining to his example the saying of Thrasybulus, that one should behold the council [τῷ θεάσει τὴν βουλὴν], so that he is free of the dye of flattery, or Gnathonism, and likewise free of the wind of boasting, or Thrasonism.
